newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus leaders agree to another meeting in Nicosia.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus leaders agree to another meeting in Nicosia.

text.p: Leaders of Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities on Monday agreed to meet again in Nicosia on Thursday to discuss humanitarian issues associated with the conflict splitting Cyprus.

The 80-minute meeting between Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides, as head of the Greek Cypriot community, and Turkish Cypriot community leader Rauf Denktash took place at the residence of the United Nations resident envoy to the island Gustave Feissel.

"The leaders of the two communities have had their first get-together here to discuss a number of humanitarian questions and they have agreed and decided to continue these discussions this coming Thursday," Feissel said at the entrance of his house, flanked by the two leaders.
Feissel declined to reveal the agenda of the meeting, confining himself to saying a "number of items" were discussed.
Wearing a dark business suit, Clerides arrived at Feissel's residence first at six p.m. (1500 GMT), followed two minutes later by Denktash.
The two leaders emerged 10 minutes later, where they gave a customary handshake for cameras in the presence of Feissel.
Asked what he expected from the meeting, Denktash replied: "Some beautiful cakes and some tea."
It is the first time the two leaders have met on home territory in nearly three years, although their offices are a five-minute drive away -- albeit cluttered with barbed wire.
Another two meetings are expected to follow.
Feissel's home is on the edge of the compound of what was once Nicosia airport. It became a U.N. protected zone after 1974.
The meeting was held two weeks after a series of U.N.-sponsored talks in upstate New York aimed at reviving negotiations on establishing a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation on the island.
A second round of talks is tentatively scheduled to take place in Montreux, Switzerland, in mid August.

The Greek Cypriot side has already committed itself to attending the talks. Asked whether he would be going to Switzerland, Denktash answered: "I will be meeting my government and party leaders on Wednesday."
Denktash heads a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in the north that is recognised only by Ankara.

Cyprus has been partitioned since troops from Turkey invaded the north of the island in 1974 in reaction to a Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia engineered by the junta then ruling Greece. Some 30,000 troops are stationed there.

The Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both communities broke apart amid violence that resulted in the dispatch of a U.N. peacekeeping force that is still on the island.
